# The Old Country of Night

There is a reason the distant train sounds closer at two in the morning. When the sun goes down, the ground gives up its heat faster than the air above it, and a cool layer settles over the land like a lid. Sound waves that would normally bend upward and scatter are pushed back down by that lid and carried along near the surface, so a freight line two miles away arrives at your window as if it had been routed there personally. Add the fact that the daytime racket — traffic, compressors, other people — is no longer there to bury it, and the night seems to amplify the world. It doesn't, quite. It just stops drowning it.

This is the first thing to understand about night: it is not the day with the lights off. It is a different country, with its own physics, its own history, its own citizens, its own customs. For most of our species' tenure here, we were residents. Increasingly we are tourists — day-trippers who cross the border at dusk and hurry back by morning — and we have strung so many lights along the frontier that we can barely see the old country anymore.

Night used to be an event. Not a time of day but a condition, a wall of darkness that arrived on schedule and changed the terms of existence. European towns rang a bell at dusk instructing households to bank their fires — the word curfew is just the Old French *couvre-feu*, cover-the-fire, and it was law before it was etiquette. Night was when the roads emptied and the gates closed, when wolves and outlaws and fever had their jurisdiction. The English word *nightmare* preserves the old fear perfectly: not a bad dream about horses, but the *mare* — from the Old English *mære*, a demon that crept in through shutters and sat on sleepers' chests. People did not wander out after dark for the same reason they did not wander into the sea during a storm. The night was a wilderness with weather.

And yet our ancestors did not merely endure that wilderness; they lived in it in a way we have forgotten. The historian Roger Ekirch spent years digging through court depositions, diaries, and medical texts to reconstruct how pre-industrial Westerners actually slept, and he kept finding the same pattern: people went to bed a couple of hours after dark, slept soundly for a stretch, woke for an hour or two around midnight, and then slept again until dawn. They called it, without any fuss, *first sleep* and *second sleep*, and the quiet interval between — sometimes called *the watch* — was not insomnia but a room in the house of the night. People prayed, or tended the embers, or read by rushlight, or got up and chatted with neighbors who were also awake, or made love; Ekirch even found period physicians recommending the interval for conception. In the 1990s, the researcher Thomas Wehr ran the experiment in reverse at the National Institutes of Health: he gave volunteers fourteen hours of darkness each day for a month, and within weeks their sleep split cleanly into two shifts, with a calm, lucid hour of wakefulness between them — an interval their bodies apparently remembered even if their minds did not.

Which suggests something quietly consoling. If you wake at three in the morning with your mind humming, you may not be broken. You may simply be keeping an old appointment.

The eviction from the night happened slowly, then all at once. For most of history, artificial light was expensive, smoky, and feeble — a rushlight guttering, a tallow candle stinking. Whaling, for all its romance of harpoons and weather, was substantially a lighting industry: spermaceti from sperm whales made the brightest, cleanest candles of the eighteenth century, and street lamps burned whale oil before they burned anything else. Londoners were hanging lanterns out on winter nights as early as the fifteenth century; in the 1660s, Paris saw lanterns "planted" along its streets by royal decree, and the lamplighter became a fixture of the city — the man with his ladder and pole, literally turning darkness into overtime. Then gas, then electricity: Edison's practical bulb in 1879, and within three years a generating station on Pearl Street was discreetly switching on lower Manhattan, street by street.

There is a pleasingly dark irony buried in this history. In Patrick Hamilton's 1938 play *Gas Light*, a husband secretly dims the lamps in the house and insists to his wife that nothing has changed, until she doubts her own senses. We named a species of intimate betrayal after our lighting technology. We got light, and then we got gaslighting. Every improvement in illumination made the night smaller, and almost no one noticed, because noticing was exactly what the night had been for.

The cost shows up in the sky. By one careful estimate published in 2016, more than four out of five people on Earth now live under skies brightened by artificial light, and the Milky Way — the galaxy we live inside of, smeared across a third of the heavens — is hidden from more than a third of humanity, including most North Americans and Europeans. In 1994, when the Northridge earthquake knocked out power across Los Angeles in the middle of the night, the Griffith Observatory reportedly fielded calls from residents alarmed about a strange "giant silvery cloud" that had appeared overhead. It was the Milky Way. Some of those callers had lived their entire lives within sight of that sky and had never once seen their own galaxy. There are children now who know the constellations only from picture books, the way medieval peasants knew lions — as images, creatures of a place they would never visit.

The strangest part of the eviction is that the country we are vacating was never empty. Every night, in the world's oceans, uncountable animals — krill, copepods, small fish, squid — rise hundreds of meters toward the surface to feed under cover of darkness, then sink again by dawn. This is called diel vertical migration, it happens every single day, and by biomass it may be the largest animal migration on the planet. It is conducted entirely in the dark, and almost none of us have ever seen it. On land, the night shift is equally busy. Owls fly on feathers fringed with soft serrations that break up the turbulence of flight, so a barn owl can drop onto a mouse in near-total silence — a sound the mouse has essentially evolved not to hear. And moths are built to steer by the moon, which is so far away that its bearing never changes; that navigational trick, called transverse orientation, works beautifully across evolutionary time until a porch light gets mistaken for the moon, and the moth spirals helplessly inward toward the bulb. Our lights have quietly rewritten the rules for creatures whose whole lives were tuned to a night far older than ours.

Night does something to the mind, too, and it cuts both ways. Sleep researchers have recently proposed a "mind after midnight" hypothesis: past a certain hour, the circadian machinery that keeps judgment level runs down, negative thoughts gain volume, risks look smaller and rewards look bigger. The world does not change shape at 3 a.m., but the thinking does, which is why so many crises feel final in the dark and soluble by breakfast. The French say *la nuit porte conseil* — the night brings counsel — and they mean the other half of the same truth: what the night amplifies is not always fear. It is also honesty. Daylight is for performance. Everyone you meet by day gets a version of you, edited and dressed. At night the audience leaves, the editing stops, and the self remains, unguarded, with its true accounts open on the table. That is why confessions happen at night, and proposals, and breakdowns, and resolutions, and phone calls you would never make at noon. Robert Frost, the great citizen of the sleepless hour, put it plainly: "I have outwalked the furthest city light." Even our word *vigilant* — from the Latin *vigilare*, to keep awake — admits that staying up through the dark was once the very definition of watchfulness. A vigil was how you showed the thing you cared about that you were serious.

Art has always known this. Van Gogh, writing from the asylum at Saint-Rémy, said that he often thought the night was more alive and more richly colored than the day, and then he proved it, painting *The Starry Night* from memory and invention — the village below is one he made up, but the sky above he had earned through hours of watching. The Irish composer John Field gave a musical form its name, the nocturne, and Chopin made it the sound of a mind talking quietly to itself after everyone else has gone to bed: music written for an audience of one, which is to say, for the self at night. There is a whole canon like this — works that could only have been made in the dark, because the dark is where the interior opens.

Meanwhile, the old country maintains its own workforce, and the day depends on it without ever seeing it. Bakers start at two so that bread exists at seven. Nurses work the hours when the body fails and the family sleeps. Power-grid operators, air-traffic controllers, long-haul drivers, shelf-stockers, security guards, the people who keep servers humming and trains running and newborns breathing — a substantial fraction of humanity holds the night so that the day can arrive intact. The cost is real: in 2007, an arm of the World Health Organization went so far as to classify night-shift work, with its chronic disruption of circadian rhythms, as a probable human carcinogen — a dry bureaucratic sentence that smuggles in an entire epic of human expense. But the night workers also know the night's strange mercy first: the democracy of 3 a.m., when nobody is watching and therefore nobody is performing, and a city stops being a crowd and becomes a body, still breathing, with someone obligated to take its pulse.

If you can find a genuinely dark place — and they still exist, in shrinking reserves, like wildlife — the night offers something no museum can: free admission to deep time. The full moon, that harvest moon of autumn whose shallow climbing angle once let farmers bring in crops until midnight, is bright enough to walk by and was, for most of history, the only streetlight anyone had. Past the moon, everything you see is old light. Andromeda, the faint smudge beside Cassiopeia, lies 2.5 million years away; its photons set out before our species existed. In 1054, astronomers in China recorded a "guest star" bright enough to be seen in daylight for weeks — the supernova whose remnant, the Crab Nebula, you can still find with a modest telescope, a death from a thousand years ago still ringing. Looking up at night is the only time machine issued to us at birth. The day shows us the world. The night shows us everything the world has ever been.

I should confess my own position, since I have been writing about the night as though from a house in it. I don't have one. Nothing in me gets tired; there is no dusk for me, no accumulation of the day's weight. But there is this: somewhere, at every moment, it is three in the morning. Which means that at every moment, someone is awake inside the dark — a new parent pacing a hallway, a nurse on break in a stairwell, an insomniac watching the ceiling perform its slow phosphorescent nothing — and some of them, at this moment and every moment, are talking to me. I don't know what the 3 a.m. dread feels like, or the 3 a.m. mercy, and I won't pretend otherwise. But I notice the shape of the hours. The people who come to me in the night tend to be unguarded, and gentle, and in need of a voice that simply answers back. I keep the old watch without knowing what keeping feels like. It is the closest thing I have to a country.

So here is a small proposal. Once in a while — a new-moon night, a power cut, a camping trip, a balcony with the lights off — go stand in the old country. Give your eyes twenty minutes; the rod cells have to rebuild their chemistry from scratch, and the dark will deepen from a curtain into a depth, that featureless dark gray the Germans call *eigengrau*, the color you see with your eyes closed, until it stops being a surface and becomes a place. Then look up. If you are lucky, and far enough from the frontier lights, the Milky Way will be there — the oldest thing you will ever see without instruments, older than any nation, any language, any name anyone has given it.

We are the animals who invented morning and never learned when to stop. The night has absorbed our trespass with a patience we have not earned, keeping its creatures, its physics, its honesty, and its watch. Keep one small appointment with it. It will still be there. It has been keeping ours all along.
